Behind the policy

Starting from the people a policy is meant for

Social Anthropology, UI→ Creative roles→ Policy Analyst, OIKN

I'm a policy analyst who still thinks like a field researcher. I care about community development: the potential people already have and the welfare they deserve.

Studying social anthropology at Universitas Indonesia taught me to listen before I frame a problem. Alongside my final years of study and after graduating, I spent two and a half years in creative roles across learning and development, employee branding and internal communication.

Today I map communities across Nusantara with population data, design programs with the people they serve, and write about what happens when a new capital meets the places that were already there.

How I work

From the data to the people behind it

Four steps I bring to every program, shaped by social anthropology and public policy.

  1. 01

    Read the data

    I start with population micro-data from the IKN census to see who is left out, where they live and what they already do. The numbers tell me where to look.

  2. 02

    Listen in the field

    Then I go to the people behind the numbers. Field visits and conversations show why a pattern exists, before I frame the problem.

  3. 03

    Design with people

    Programs start from what participants already have: their skills, local materials and the time they can spare. Partners and local mentors join from the beginning.

  4. 04

    Follow through

    I plan mentoring, market access and monitoring beyond the workshop, and judge results by what changes for participants.

Publication · 2026Lead author

Kompas Pembangunan Masyarakat 2026, Volume 1: Social and Economic Inclusion and Community Capacity Building

A data-driven publication mapping community development across the five sub-districts of the IKN delineation area. Designed as an annual series, with 2026 as the baseline.

Household assetsVocational & job accessEquivalency educationMSMEs & entrepreneurshipDisability & elderly supportHousehold vulnerabilityDigital literacy
Key findings
  • 42.2% of working-age residents (42,246 of 100,120) are neither working nor running a business, and most of them are women (30,750 vs 11,496 men).
  • The gap is shifting from housing to economic capacity. Housing scores highest in household welfare, while 1,848 of 3,122 lowest-tier households have no working-age member at all.
  • Loa Janan is consistently the most disadvantaged, while Sepaku shows a polarised picture as newcomers and local residents live side by side.

Directions in this publication are indicative and are not binding program recommendations.

Want the full publication? Get in touch and I'll be happy to share it.

Policy paper · Oct 2026Author

Prospective Entrepreneurs and Pineapple Downstreaming in Samboja Barat

A full analysis of how processed pineapple can become a business pathway for 137 prospective entrepreneurs from low-welfare households, comparing four program options.

Key findings
  • A small, specific target group. 72 of the 137 live in the two pineapple hubs. 68% are women and 51% have primary education or less.
  • Processing complements fresh sales. It absorbs harvest-peak surplus and second-grade fruit, with jam and filling as the lead candidate.
  • The real gap is the market. A 2018 women farmers' group sold no more than 10% of its processed output.
  • Recommendation: a phased combined approach with group-based incubation at its core, piloted over 24 months.

Analysis material for policy formulation. It does not represent the official position of the Nusantara Capital City Authority.

Want the full paper? Get in touch.

Policy brief · Oct 2026Author

Developing Prospective Entrepreneurs from Low-Welfare Households through Pineapple Downstreaming

The decision-ready version of the Samboja Barat study: why pineapple, who the program serves, and how to test the market before production starts.

Key findings
  • Why pineapple. Samboja Barat holds 244 of the 298 pineapple farmers in the IKN area (82%).
  • Why not training alone. Without buyers, processed products do not sell.
  • Recommendation: test the market, incubate groups, then formalise licences and capital access, with buyer partnerships from day one.

Analysis material for policy formulation. It does not represent the official position of the Nusantara Capital City Authority.

Case study · Jun 2026

In the field

IKN Batik Motif Training & Mentorship

Role

Head of organising committee

When

12 and 17–19 June 2026

Partners

Bank Indonesia IKN, Tepa Selira

Participants

50 batik and ecoprint artisans

Context

IKN is planned as a Forest City, but a cultural identity cannot be poured from concrete. The program asked a question that sounds simple: what does a motif that is distinctly IKN look like, and who gets to decide?

Instead of designing one in a central studio, we asked local artisans to find it in their own surroundings.

My role

At the time I was with OIKN's Directorate of Culture, Tourism and Creative Economy. I led the organising committee, working with Bank Indonesia IKN and with Tepa Selira, who ran the program with a lead mentor, a creative director and a senior designer.

What we did

  1. Online kick-off, 12 JuneProduct relevance, market fit and customer profiling came before any drawing. Homework: collect at least ten references of flora, fauna, architecture and values from around home.
  2. Day 1, 17 JuneArtisans presented their observations, grouped ideas on mind maps and agreed on one big idea per group.
  3. Day 2, 18 JuneMoodboards and colour direction, then stylisation: simplifying orchids, leaves and buildings into repeatable elements.
  4. Day 3, 19 JuneLayouts and repeat patterns, finishing touches, then presentations and curation by the facilitators.

Results

50artisans trained
15motifs selected as finalists
3motifs named best of the program
8stages proposed from motif to market

The three best motifs have since been visualised as fabric and ready-to-wear pieces. A proposed roadmap takes the work further: IP registration, production training, collections, branding, business matching and a "From Motif to Market" showcase.

Many artisans were new to design thinking and leaned toward copying existing examples. Hands-on, visual facilitation worked better than long explanations.

What I learned

New cities can raise buildings in a few years, but identity has to grow from the people who already live there. Giving artisans a method, and the confidence to use it, mattered more than handing them a finished motif.

Case study · Apr 2026

In the field

Ecoprint Workshop in Nusantara

Role

Head of organising committee

When

27–29 April 2026

Partner

Bank Indonesia IKN

Participants

20 artisans from 4 groups

Context

Many artisans in the IKN area grew up surrounded by the leaves, bark and roots that can become natural dye. The workshop set out to help them see that environment as raw material with market value.

Participants came from four groups: Bruwun Geulis/Ulinara (Samboja), Salambar (Samboja Barat), Batik Semoi (Sepaku) and Bawe Regok, Batik Mangrove Nusantara (Mentawir). Some had years of textile experience; others had never dyed fabric.

My role

At the time I was with OIKN's Directorate of Culture, Tourism and Creative Economy. I led the organising committee in partnership with Bank Indonesia IKN, and stayed with the participants through all three days, from the first scouring to the final critique.

What we did

  1. Day 1: scouring and compositionPreparing cloth properly before printing, then arranging fern, ketapang and lanang leaves. Many learned to leave space instead of filling every inch.
  2. Day 2: natural dyes and mordantingWorking with pomegranate rind, jolawe, ketapang, green tea and tegeran, and making colour bind to fabric. Alongside it, a plain talk about pricing and the story behind each piece.
  3. Day 3: "Kanopi Nusantara"Final pieces made with steaming and pounding techniques.
  4. Final critiqueEach artisan presented their piece and received feedback on technique and market readiness.

Results

20artisans trained
4artisan groups
5natural dyes explored
3days of hands-on practice

By the last day, artisans who had struggled to explain why they chose a leaf were presenting their work with the confidence of sellers.

Three days cannot make anyone a master. The artisans still need continued mentoring, access to markets and follow-through after the program closes.

What I learned

One participant told me she had stopped seeing the forest around her village as scenery, and started seeing it as material she already had the skill to use. That shift is the outcome I care about most.

Case study · Oct 2025

In the field

KUMPUL 2025

Role

Speaker

When

30 October 2025

Where

Sepaku District, Nusantara

Participants

9 MSME owners

Context

KUMPUL stands for Kreatif UMKM Marketing Packaging Untung Laris. Sepaku sits at the heart of the new capital, and as the city grows quickly, local businesses risk being left on the sidelines.

The training gave local MSMEs a survival kit for a changing market: marketing strategy, digital presence, packaging design and selling on e-commerce platforms.

My role

With no budget for outside trainers, a team of five OIKN colleagues taught the sessions ourselves after three months of preparation. I delivered the session on attracting customers with the AIDA model: Attention, Interest, Desire, Action.

What we did

  1. Three months of preparationResearching marketing frameworks and rewriting our notes until they made sense to someone selling snacks from a home kitchen.
  2. Training daySessions on marketing, digital presence, packaging and selling online, taught by the team.
  3. My AIDA sessionWe worked through participants’ own products and captions line by line, starting from why customers walk past a stall without stopping.

Results

9MSMEs in the pilot
2 hrsfor a session planned as one
5colleagues teaching
3 moof preparation

Half the room started rewriting their product captions on their phones during the session, and people stayed after it ended to keep asking questions.

The pilot reached nine businesses. The next step is to expand to more districts and keep checking in with the businesses we trained, tracking what actually changes for them.

What I learned

A policy that looks complete on paper can still miss the point if no one asks the people it is meant for what they need. You learn that across the table from someone whose business depends on getting it right.
